title: Not all lump sums are unconstitutional
primary_topics: Two-part question reframing: not whether lump sums are constitutional but whether THESE 2023 lump sums function as PDAF-style pork
Belgica v. Ochoa (Nov. 19, 2013) -- first Bernabe decision banishing PDAF and CDF
Belgica v. Executive Secretary (Oct. 8, 2019) -- Bernabe's second decision clarifying lump sums permissible 'as long as singular appropriation purpose'
Singular-correspondence doctrine: lump sum functions as line-item if all underlying programs/projects share one classifiable purpose
Reframing of CJ's Oct. 17 column query to Senator Pimentel in light of the 2019 clarification

Ochoa quoted at length on the six grounds: (a) violated separation of powers via non-oversight post-enactment authority; (b) violated non-delegability via personal discretionary funds; (c) flouted presentment by non-textualized appropriations bill items, denying President item-veto; (d) impaired public accountability via legislator stake in budget execution; (e) subverted local autonomy via national-officer intervention in local affairs; (f) transgressed non-delegability again via Malampaya Fund / PD 1869 unbounded presidential redirection

Belgica 2019 standard: lump sums constitutional 'as long as the lump-sum amount(s) (are) meant as a funding source for multiple programs, projects or activities that may all be clearly classified as falling under one singular appropriation purpose'
Singular-correspondence doctrine: lump sum 'effectively functions as a line-item' if compliant
Generality/specificity allowed by Congress provided it 'does not negate the President's proper exercise of his item veto power'

Result of PDAF's amorphous lumping: no discernible item left for presidential veto -- 'constitutionally infirm'

stances.claim: The current 'ruckus on the gargantuan lump sums' -- especially the P9.3 billion 'confidential and intelligence funds' in the proposed P5.268 trillion 2023 budget -- evokes 'a penumbra of PDAF,' but the question whether they are unconstitutional requires the doctrinal distinction the Court made between Belgica v. Ochoa (2013) and the less-known Belgica v. Executive Secretary (2019).

Belgica v. Ochoa (Nov. 19, 2013), Justice Perlas-Bernabe's 'monumental' decision, banished the Pork Barrel / PDAF / CDF system on six interlocking grounds: violated separation of powers (legislators wielding 'non-oversight, post-enactment authority' in budget execution); violated non-delegability of legislative power (personal discretionary funds); flouted presentment (non-textualized items denying President item-veto); impaired public accountability (legislator stake in budget execution they oversee); subverted local autonomy (national officers intervening in local affairs); and transgressed non-delegability again (presidential redirection of energy / 'priority infrastructure' funds to other purposes).
stances.rhetorical_move: verbatim six-ground enumeration from Belgica v. Ochoa

stances.claim: The less-known Belgica v. Executive Secretary (Oct. 8, 2019) -- also Bernabe-penned -- rejected the per-se-unconstitutional contention and established the 'singular correspondence' doctrine: a lump sum is constitutional 'as long as the lump-sum amount(s) (are) meant as a funding source for multiple programs, projects or activities that may all be clearly classified as falling under one singular appropriation purpose.' The lump sum then 'effectively functions as a line-item' that does not negate the President's item-veto power.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-clarification recital with quoted operative language

stances.claim: The 2013 PDAF's P24.79 billion was constitutionally infirm because it funded 'multiple unrelated purposes' -- 'scholarships, medical missions, assistance to indigents, preservation of historical materials, construction of roads, flood control, etc.' -- all under the 'vague and amorphous term Priority Development Assistance Fund,' which let individual legislators decide whatever 'priority' meant and 'left no discernible item for the exercise of the President's veto power.' A lump sum is unconstitutional when it both (a) funds multiple unrelated purposes and (b) eliminates the President's item-veto.
stances.confidence: asserted with named-figure ($24.79B) and verbatim itemization

stances.claim: With the Bernabe clarification, the test for the 2023 lump sums (including the P9.3B CIF and the DPWH's P544B) is whether each lump sum funds programs falling under 'one singular appropriation purpose' that preserves item-veto. CJ reframes his Oct. 17 query: 'will the esteemed Senator Pimentel be able to reply to my query now?'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban returns to the 'ruckus on the gargantuan lump sums' -- especially the P9.3 billion 'confidential and intelligence funds' in the proposed P5.268 trillion 2023 national budget -- that evoke 'a penumbra of PDAF,' as he had argued in his October 17 column. He recalls that Belgica v. Ochoa (November 19, 2013), the 'monumental' decision penned by Justice Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe, unanimously banished the Pork Barrel System / Priority Development Assistance Fund (PDAF) / Countrywide Development Fund (CDF) on six interlocking grounds quoted verbatim -- violating separation of powers (legislators wielding 'non-oversight, post-enactment authority' in budget execution); violating non-delegability of legislative power (personal discretionary funds 'from which they are able to fund specific projects which they themselves determine'); flouting presentment (non-textualized items denying the President item-veto); impairing public accountability (legislator stake in budget execution they oversee); subverting genuine local autonomy (national officers intervening in local affairs); and once more transgressing non-delegability (presidential authority to redirect funds 'intended by law to energy-related purposes only to other purposes he may deem fit'). CJ had closed his October 17 column with the question whether the 2023 lump sums 'could be scuttled using Belgica v. Ochoa' and asked, 'Perhaps, Senator Pimentel can?' He received no answer from Sen. Koko Pimentel -- but did receive an email from the retired Justice Bernabe herself, referring him to her 2022 book 'Perlas-Bernabe On Law and Justice,' which records that less than a year after Belgica v. Ochoa a petition was filed seeking to declare ALL lump-sum appropriations unconstitutional per se. The SC rejected the contention in Belgica v. Executive Secretary (October 8, 2019), clarifying that some lump-sum appropriations remain constitutional 'as long as the lump-sum amount(s) (are) meant as a funding source for multiple programs, projects or activities that may all be clearly classified as falling under one singular appropriation purpose.' Under this 'doctrine of singular correspondence,' the lump sum 'effectively functions as a line-item' compatible with the President's item-veto, regardless of the generality or specificity of the singular purpose. By contrast, the 2013 PDAF's P24.79 billion funded 'multiple unrelated purposes' -- 'scholarships, medical missions, assistance to indigents, preservation of historical materials, construction of roads, flood control, etc.' -- all under 'the vague and amorphous term Priority Development Assistance Fund,' leaving 'no more discernible item' for the President's veto and rendering the appropriation 'constitutionally infirm.' With 'that scholarly clarification by the lady justice,' CJ renews his query to Pimentel: 'will the esteemed Senator Pimentel be able to reply to my query now?'
